content: Bronchiectasis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the airways, characterized by a recurring cycle of respiratory bacterial infections. These infections are commonly associated with symptoms such as persistent coughing, production of sputum, and a significant reduction in the patient’s quality of life. Antibiotics are the cornerstone of treatment for managing exacerbations of bronchiectasis. Current evidence suggests that inhaled antibiotics may be more effective in eradicating infectious organisms and may carry a lower risk of promoting antibiotic resistance compared to oral antibiotics. However, it remains uncertain whether oral or inhaled antibiotics are superior in terms of overall efficacy and safety. The objective of this review was to evaluate and compare the effectiveness and safety of oral versus inhaled antibiotics in treating both adults and children with bronchiectasis. The review aimed to assess these treatments for both short-term use (less than four weeks) during acute exacerbations and long-term use (four weeks or more) as a preventive measure. Studies involving participants who had received continuous or high-dose antibiotics immediately prior to the trial, or those diagnosed with conditions such as cystic fibrosis, sarcoidosis, active allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, or active non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections, were excluded from consideration. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Airways Group's Specialised Register, which includes trial reports from databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, AMED, and PsycINFO, as well as hand-searched respiratory journals and conference abstracts. Additional searches were performed on ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO trials portal. The search was completed in March 2018, with no restrictions on the language of publication. Two independent reviewers applied the inclusion criteria to the search results. They also planned to extract data, assess the risk of bias, and evaluate the overall quality of evidence using the GRADE framework. Efforts were to be made to contact study authors for missing data, and results were to be reported with 95% confidence intervals. The search yielded 313 unique records from databases and an additional 21 records from trial registries. After screening titles and abstracts, 307 records were excluded. A further 27 records were excluded after full-text review. Ultimately, no studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. The authors concluded that there is currently no evidence to determine whether oral antibiotics are more effective than inhaled antibiotics, or vice versa, for the treatment of bronchiectasis. The European Respiratory Society (ERS) guidelines for bronchiectasis provide a practical framework for the use of long-term antibiotics, but further research is urgently needed. Specifically, studies comparing inhaled and oral antibiotic therapies in patients with frequent exacerbations are necessary to determine which approach is most effective in preventing exacerbations, improving quality of life, reducing treatment burden, and minimizing antibiotic resistance.
